title: Which guesses were real accounts
briefing: Most of the usernames in the brute force do not exist here, and sshd turned them away as `invalid user`. The ones that DO exist are the real exposure: they held passwords an attacker could guess.
Intersect two lists: the names the attacker tried, and the accounts that exist on this host with their uids. Report the overlap.

lesson.p: Set operations on sorted files. `comm` compares two sorted lists of lines. `join` matches two sorted files on a key field, like a database join. `paste` puts files side by side, or folds one file onto a single line. `column -t` lines up the result.

flags: three columns: only in A / only in B / in both (indented with tabs)
suppress columns 1 and 2: the lines in BOTH (intersection)
suppress columns 2 and 3: lines only in A (A minus B)
for each key (field 1) found in both files, print the key and the other fields from both
also print lines from A that have no match in B (a left outer join)
comma-separated; key is field 2 of file 1 and field 1 of file 2
lines of A and B side by side / all lines of A on one line, joined by spaces
bash process substitution: the output of a pipeline used as if it were a file
align whitespace-separated columns; `-s,` to split on commas

lesson.note: `comm` and `join` need input sorted on the key, in the SAME locale. Unsorted input gives missing rows, with at best a warning. `sort -u` each side with `LC_ALL=C` (Level 4) before you join.

examples.title: Three columns of comm

stages.why: Both files are already sorted. Column 1: only in team A. Column 2 (one tab): only in team B. Column 3 (two tabs): on both teams.

examples.output:
alice
		bob
carol
		dave
erin
	frank
	grace

stages.why: Hide column 2 (only in B) and column 3 (in both): what is left is only in A.

examples.title: Join two lists on the user name

stages.why: Field 1 of each file is the key. Each user in both files gets one line: name, uid (from file 1), shell (from file 2).
carol has no shell entry and zed has no uid, so neither appears: join prints only matches by default.

examples.title: Keep the unmatched rows, then align

stages.why: Also print rows from file 1 with no match. carol appears with no shell, which is a gap worth asking about.
Line the columns up so the gap is easy to see.

examples.title: Fold a list onto one line

stages.why: Serial: join all lines of the file instead of pairing them with another file.
Put a comma between them. Handy for building `-u alice,bob` style arguments or a ticket summary.

challenge.question: Which usernames that 203.0.113.66 tried in Failed password lines in var/log/secure belong to accounts that exist on this host, and what uid does each have? An account exists if it appears in a "session opened for user NAME(uid=N)" line in var/log/secure or var/log/secure-20260313.
challenge.format: Each name followed by its uid, sorted by name, all on one line separated by single spaces, for example alice 1001 bob 1002

hints: Build two sorted lists. List 1: the usernames the attacker tried, one per line, `sort -u` (you built this pipeline in Level 4). List 2: `name uid` pairs from the session lines, `sort -u`. Then intersect them on the name.

For list 2, `grep -ohE 'session opened for user [a-z_]+\(uid=[0-9]+\)'` over both secure files, then `sed -E 's/.*user ([a-z_]+)\(uid=([0-9]+)\)/\1 \2/'`. `join LIST1 LIST2` keeps the names in both and adds the uid; `paste -sd' '` puts the result on one line.

join <(grep 'Failed password' var/log/secure | grep -oE '[^ ]+ from 203\.0\.113\.66 ' | cut -d' ' -f1 | sort -u) <(grep -ohE 'session opened for user [a-z_]+\(uid=[0-9]+\)' var/log/secure* | sed -E 's/.*user ([a-z_]+)\(uid=([0-9]+)\)/\1 \2/' | sort -u) | paste -sd___

debrief.solution: join <(grep 'Failed password' var/log/secure | grep -oE '[^ ]+ from 203\.0\.113\.66 ' | cut -d' ' -f1 | sort -u) <(grep -ohE 'session opened for user [a-z_]+\(uid=[0-9]+\)' var/log/secure* | sed -E 's/.*user ([a-z_]+)\(uid=([0-9]+)\)/\1 \2/' | sort -u) | paste -sd' '
debrief.alternative: grep -ohE 'session opened for user [a-z_]+\(uid=[0-9]+\)' var/log/secure* | sed -E 's/.*user ([a-z_]+)\(uid=([0-9]+)\)/\1 \2/' | sort -u > /tmp/uids; comm -12 <(grep 'Failed password' var/log/secure | grep -oE '[^ ]+ from 203\.0\.113\.66 ' | cut -d' ' -f1 | sort -u) <(cut -d' ' -f1 /tmp/uids) | join - /tmp/uids | paste -sd' '
why: Two real accounts were in the wordlist: root and svc_backup. root is a guess on every host on the internet; it should never accept a password over SSH. svc_backup is the account that fell. A service account with a guessable password and an interactive shell is the root cause of this incident.

On a live RHEL host you would build list 2 from the account database instead: `getent passwd | cut -d: -f1,3 | tr : ' ' | sort -u`. Session lines only show accounts that have logged in; getent shows every account, including the ones nobody has used yet.

The fixes follow from the overlap: `PermitRootLogin no`, key-only SSH for service accounts (or `nologin` as their shell if they never need one), and an `AllowGroups` line in sshd's configuration so that only named groups can log in at all.
